title: The Doughnut Destroyer's Race
markdown:
Morning sun, bright as a sugar cookie, dappled Bakery Street. The lane smelled of cinnamon swirls. Shopkeepers called cheerful greetings. On a pile of gleaming timber, Siani Buttercup — a monkey of most particular habits and a scarlet bow tie that never off-duty — unrolled a banana-yellow measuring tape.

“We embark upon a grand endeavour,” he told Jun the pigeon, who sat on a crate of rope and offered a coo that might have been agreement or a polite query. “The Doughnut Destroyer shall not merely join the Great River Race. It shall dominate. Principles of air and movement never before applied to boats.”

The blueprint looked more like a complicated pastry recipe than a hull. Siani tapped strategically placed openings meant to catch breeze. Townsfolk paused with baskets of loaves, polite smiles arranged over gentle doubt. They had seen Siani’s plans before. Each had been grander, and stranger, than the last. Siani saw only an audience leaning in for the next instalment.

Building commenced under bunting already strung for race week. Every plank, every nail received direction and a commentary on strong structures and smooth sailing. His baritone bounced off Bakery Street brick. The hammer went thwack in time with the lecture. A baker paused with a tray of buns and asked whether the holes were meant for jam. Siani assured him they were meant for destiny.

“And now we secure the buoyancy chamber.” He fastened a large circular piece of wood into the hull, brow furrowed. “The curve pushes water away. The exact angle is key to… to… well. To floating.” The science, if it had ever fully arrived, took a short holiday. He measured twice with the yellow tape, announced the numbers as if they were headlines, and hammered anyway.

A loud honk cut the street. Agnes the Goose waddled in, sturdy, determined, feathers ruffled by the morning, beady eyes fixed on the peculiar timber as if it had insulted waterfowl everywhere.

“An unexpected guest,” Siani sighed. “A local commentator with a striking lack of appreciation. Jun, if you would.”

Jun puffed, a grey shadow of helpfulness, and nudged Agnes with a wing. She honked a low rumble of disagreement, gave the hull a final curious peck, and ambled off. Siani tutted professionally. The bow tie remained a tiny beacon of order.

The pattern repeated through the week, almost comically on time. Siani attached what he called air-catching sails — large, bright pinwheels salvaged from a forgotten carousel, crimson and gold and azure, the same colours as the street’s festive bunting. Agnes returned. She honked at the spinning blades as if colour itself were a navigational insult. Siani halted to deliver a stern report to the unheeding planks. “A persistent problem. This goose possesses an aversion to innovative turning mechanisms. A narrative challenge.” He paused, as if for a commercial, then resumed.

Jun guided Agnes away again and again, a silent contrast to Siani’s pronouncements, sometimes with a crumb, sometimes with sheer patience. Children counted the honks. The bunting fluttered. The street watched the ballet of creation and minor chaos and went home with stories that were not quite the ones Siani was broadcasting. Siani saw only vision, each honk a dramatic pause before triumph. The pinwheels turned in every breeze, a motif of circles: doughnut hull, colander openings, spinning colour, even the tape curling back on itself when he let go.

Race day filled the riverbanks with flags and faces, a sea of picnic baskets and fluttering colour against sparkling water. The Doughnut Destroyer sat beside Siani, a vessel of peculiar shape and even more peculiar confidence. The pinwheels were poised. The openings looked like colanders offering views of sky. The hull was suspiciously round, like a giant doughnut left in the sun and then asked, firmly, to be a boat.

Siani cleared his throat and adjusted the bow tie with a flourish. “Esteemed participants and spectators. We are poised to witness a triumph of scientific endeavour. The unusual shape is not a mistake. It is a feature. A bold step from the ordinary, designed for maximum… impact.” A judge wrote something down that was probably not impact.

The signal gathered itself. A piercing honk arrived first. Agnes waddled directly in front of the Destroyer and honked with urgency, then nudged the boat with her beak. It wobbled toward the water.

The crowd gasped, a ripple of anticipation mixed with the particular worry reserved for homemade boats. The Destroyer slid in. It bobbed. For a breath it seemed ready to become a story about sinking. Then the pinwheels caught the light breeze and whirled faster, a dizzy blur of festival colour. The colander openings channelled air and shoved. The boat did not sail in any sense taught by rivers. It was pushed. And it moved.

Laughter warmed the banks. Siani’s jaw loosened. The bow tie sagged like a flower that had heard the weather report too late. Jun, on his shoulder, cooed and nudged, a small acknowledgement that the universe kept its own jokes.

The Doughnut Destroyer glided with absurd grace. It did not cut waves; it surfed them on its own wind-catching nonsense. Agnes honked from the bank as if she had conducted the whole symphony and was now taking a bow.

Siani, after a stunned quiet, chuckled — a crack in the broadcast face. “Well. That is one way to make a splash.”

The Destroyer did not win. It stole the afternoon anyway, a round idea spinning down a river that had expected something pointed. The bunting, which had begun the morning as mere festival colour, winked in the same crimson, gold, and azure as the pinwheels. Jun’s coo settled in Siani’s ear. Agnes preened. Bakery Street smelled of cinnamon still, and of river, and of a boat that had decided floating was a kind of pastry after all.
characters: Siani Buttercup (a fussy monkey boat builder), Jun (a pigeon friend)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing story for older children
